purpose: Predeclared author-crafted diagnostic of standard written English subject-verb agreement and word order. Freeze before scoring; no model outputs informed these pairs.
limitations: Synthetic teacher-forced sentence likelihood diagnostic, not a standardized grammar benchmark or independent evidence of general grammar competence.
Labels concern standard written English; they do not evaluate dialects or speakers.
Preference may reflect lexical frequency or memorized patterns rather than grammatical abstraction. Equal character length removes a simple length difference, not every confound.
Agreement pairs intentionally change a same-length verb; word-order pairs preserve the exact character and word multisets.
All pairs fit the64-character model context. No claim about long-distance syntax, generation coherence, or release readiness.
Do not use these pairs to train, tune, select checkpoints, or claim a fresh independent test after repeated inspection.

scoring_definition.unit: Character token using the existing fixed51-character vocabulary.
scoring_definition.sentence_log_probability: Sum log P(sentence[t] | sentence[:t]) for t=1..len(sentence)-1, using causal teacher forcing and natural logarithms. The first character is conditioning context and is not scored. No BOS, EOS, padding, or extra newline is added.
scoring_definition.pair_margin: grammatical_sentence_log_probability minus ungrammatical_sentence_log_probability; positive favors the grammatical sentence.
scoring_definition.accuracy: 1 for positive margin,0 for negative margin,0.5 for exact tie. Report every margin and aggregate by category and overall; no significance claim.
scoring_definition.controls: Both members have identical total character length and identical initial character. Score each complete sentence without truncation, padding, or length normalization. Use eval mode and no_grad.

pairs.rationale: First-person singular I takes am, not is.
First-person singular agreement in a predicate-adjective frame.
Third-person singular He takes is, not am.
Third-person singular agreement in a predicate-adjective frame.
Third-person singular She takes is, not am.
Third-person singular agreement reuses the happy lexical frame with a different subject.
Plural We permits are; was does not agree in standard written English.
Plural agreement in the tired lexical frame.
Plural They permits are; was does not agree in standard written English.
Plural agreement reuses the happy lexical frame.

pairs.grammatical: The dog was in the park.
pairs.ungrammatical: The dog are in the park.
pairs.rationale: Singular dog permits was; are does not agree.
Singular cat permits was; are does not agree.
Singular bird permits was; are does not agree.
Singular boy permits was; are does not agree.
Plural dogs permits are; was does not agree; counters the singular animal frames.

pairs.grammatical: The cats are in the park.
pairs.ungrammatical: The cats was in the park.
pairs.rationale: Plural cats permits are; was does not agree; counters the singular animal frames.
Swapping the subject noun and finite verb breaks the subject noun phrase.
Reverses dog/cat lexical roles while preserving the same word-order error.

pairs.grammatical: A girl has a red ball.
pairs.ungrammatical: A girl a has red ball.
pairs.rationale: Moving the object determiner before the finite verb breaks both verb and object phrase order.

pairs.grammatical: A boy has a blue box.
pairs.ungrammatical: A boy a has blue box.
pairs.rationale: Same determiner/verb inversion with different nouns and color.

pairs.grammatical: The bird sat on a tree.
pairs.ungrammatical: The bird on sat a tree.
pairs.rationale: Moving the preposition before the verb leaves an ill-formed prepositional phrase.

pairs.grammatical: The cat sat on a bed.
pairs.ungrammatical: The cat on sat a bed.
pairs.rationale: Same preposition/verb inversion in a familiar animal frame.
Object determiner cannot precede found in this ordinary declarative sentence.
Counters the pronoun and object of the same determiner/verb error.

pairs.grammatical: The girl went to the park.
pairs.ungrammatical: The girl to went the park.
pairs.rationale: The preposition to cannot precede went while its object remains after went.

pairs.grammatical: The boy went to the shop.
pairs.ungrammatical: The boy to went the shop.
pairs.rationale: Same preposition/verb inversion with another subject and destination.
Swapping with and played breaks the verb/prepositional phrase order.
Same verb/preposition inversion with a different pronoun and object.
